alignment.note: Greek and Latin open with the coordinating conjunction καί/Et ('and'), whereas the Peshitta uses the postpositive adversative-connective particle ܕܝܢ ('but/and now'), which it places after the fronted adverb ܠܘܩܕܡ. The functional connective force is comparable, but the Syriac nuances the link as mildly contrastive.
πρῶτον / ܠܘܩܕܡ / primum ('first'); the Peshitta fronts the adverb to the head of the clause, a typical Syriac word-order preference, while Greek and Latin position it medially.

Greek δεῖ and Latin oportet are impersonal verbs of necessity ('it is necessary'), whereas the Peshitta renders the obligation with the verbal adjective ܥܬܝܕܐ ('it is destined/about to be'), shifting the modality slightly toward futurity and divine appointment rather than bare necessity.
κηρυχθῆναι / ܕܬܬܟܪܙ / prædicari ('to be proclaimed'); all three render the passive infinitive, the Syriac using its Ethpaal imperfect within a complementiser construction.

Greek τὸ εὐαγγέλιον and Latin Evangelium employ the loan-noun 'gospel/good news', whereas the Peshitta uses the native Semitic ܣܒܪܬܐ ('good tidings/proclamation') bearing the first-person suffix ('my gospel' in some witnesses), a lexical rather than borrowed rendering of the same concept.

εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη / ܒܟܠܗܘܢ ܥܡܡܐ / in omnes gentes ('to/among all the nations'); Greek and Latin use a goal-marking preposition (εἰς/in 'into'), while the Peshitta uses ܒ- ('in/among'), a locative nuance, with the noun ܥܡܡܐ standing for the Gentile peoples.
